analysis.one_liner: Sets deadlines and binding arbitration for the first union contract after workers organize.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 230-193 on June 9, 2026, with every voting Democrat and 20 Republicans in favor, and it now sits with the Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: When workers vote to join a union, getting the first contract often takes a year or longer, and the bill's findings say employers can use that delay to wear workers down. This bill sets a clock: bargaining must start within 10 days of the request, a federal mediator steps in after 90 days without a deal, and after 30 more days a three-person arbitration panel can impose a contract that binds both sides for two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Newly organized workers and their unions gain the most. Instead of waiting an average of 465 days from a union vote to a first contract, they would get mediation and then binding arbitration on a fixed timeline. The arbitrators must weigh workers' cost of living, whether wages can support their families, and what comparable employers pay, so the imposed contract is aimed at liveable terms. Workers also gain because employers must keep current wages, hours, and conditions in place while bargaining goes on.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Newly unionized workers and their unions

how_it_helps.text: Bargaining must begin within 10 days after an employer receives a written request from a newly recognized or certified union, or a longer period the parties agree on.

If there is no agreement after 90 days, either side can ask the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service to mediate; if mediation fails within 30 days, a three-person arbitration panel imposes a contract binding for two years.
Arbitrators must base the contract on the employer's finances, employees' cost of living, whether wages can sustain workers and their families, and what other employers in the same business pay.
Employers must maintain current wages, hours, and terms of employment while bargaining, and the duty to bargain continues as long as the union has not been decertified.

The bill's findings cite a 2021 study finding an average of 465 days between a successful union vote and a first contract, and state that these delays primarily benefit employers opposed to the union.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially companies where workers have just organized, bear the cost: they lose the leverage of slow-walking negotiations, must keep existing pay and conditions locked in during bargaining, and may have a contract imposed on them by arbitrators. Arbitration and mediation costs and the imposed terms may ultimately show up in business costs, which employers may pass along or absorb in hiring.

drawbacks.text: Binding arbitration can impose contract terms neither side agreed to, which employers argue weakens genuine bargaining and forces terms they consider unaffordable or poorly suited to their business.
The imposed contract binds both sides for two years and can only be changed by written consent of both parties, limiting flexibility if business conditions change.

The requirement to maintain current wages, hours, and conditions during negotiations and the continued bargaining duty limit employer discretion over workplace changes while a first contract is pending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For newly organized workers the gain is large and direct: a first contract on a fixed timeline instead of a delay that the bill itself says benefits employers. The costs fall on employers, and the arbitration mechanism is blunt — a panel with one union pick, one employer pick, and one neutral member can set wages and terms for an entire workforce, and the employer-focused factors may not capture every small business's situation. On balance the design targets a documented problem (an average 465-day wait) with a process that still lets the parties settle on their own at any point before arbitration.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote on June 9, 2026, and the Senate received it the next day; no Senate action has been taken yet.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 16, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, where no further committee action is recorded.
It was instead brought to the floor under a special rule (H. Res. 1140), which allowed one hour of debate and an up-or-down vote without a committee markup.
On June 9, 2026, the House passed it 230-193: 210 of 210 voting Democrats voted yes, and 20 of 212 voting Republicans joined them; the Senate's only independent member voted no.
The Senate received the bill on June 10, 2026; no further action is recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, newly organized workers and their unions, who gained full House passage with near-unanimous Democratic support. Nothing changes in law unless the Senate passes the bill and the President signs it, so employers resisting union contracts are better off only if the Senate lets it sit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Newly organized workers and unions, so far

for.name: Rep. Donald Norcross
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Workforce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through House passage.

for.name: 110 House cosponsors (93 Democrats, 17 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing before the vote.

for.name: House leadership under Speaker Mike Johnson
for.role: Scheduled the floor vote via rule H. Res. 1140
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under a special rule despite most Republicans opposing it, allowing the 230-193 passage vote.

against.name: 192 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against passage, 192 to 20, leaving the bill dependent on Democratic votes.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was received in the Senate on June 10, 2026.

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Long opposed mandatory first-contract arbitration as a government imposition of contract terms on unwilling employers.

sides.party_line_note: Support split almost perfectly by party: all 210 voting Democrats and 20 of 212 voting Republicans voted yes, one independent voted no, for a 230-193 passage.

industries.industry: Nonunion private employers facing organizing drives
industries.note: The bill removes their main advantage in first-contract talks — the ability to delay for a year or more — and subjects them to mediation and potentially binding arbitration. For ordinary people the industry's interest runs against workers' right to a timely contract.
Unions gain a fixed path to a first contract, which is the stage where organizing campaigns most often stall; faster contracts also make union representation more valuable to prospective members.

industries.industry: Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service and labor arbitrators
industries.note: The bill gives the agency a new statutory mediation-and-referral role and creates demand for three-person arbitration panels, expanding work for neutrals in this field.

analysis.trajectory: The bill passed the House with 230 votes but with only about 9% of House Republicans in favor, and no Senate companion action is recorded. Labor-law changes of this kind generally need 60 votes to clear a Senate procedural hurdle, and Senate leadership has not scheduled consideration. The most likely path is that the bill sits in the Senate without a vote until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
